## 6. The converse (optional — not needed for the campaign)

**Theorem 1.3.** Let `X` be compact, `f : X → X` continuous, and suppose that for every
`φ ∈ C(X)` there is `c(φ) ∈ ℝ` with `A_n φ → c(φ)` uniformly on `X`. Then `f` has a unique
invariant probability measure.

*Proof.* `c` is linear, positive (`φ ≥ 0 ⇒ c(φ) ≥ 0`) and `c(1) = 1`; by the Riesz representation
theorem on the compact space `X` there is `μ ∈ P(X)` with `c(φ) = ∫φ dμ`. For `φ ∈ C(X)`,
`A_n(φ∘f) x = A_n φ (f x) + O(1/n)`, so `c(φ∘f) = c(φ)`, i.e. `∫φ d(f_*μ) = ∫φ dμ` for all
continuous `φ`, so `f_*μ = μ`. If `ν` is invariant then `∫φ dν = ∫ A_nφ dν` for every `n`
(invariance), and `A_nφ → c(φ)` uniformly, so `∫φ dν = c(φ) = ∫φ dμ` for all `φ ∈ C(X)`, hence
`ν = μ`. ∎

The step `ν = μ` from equal integrals against *continuous* test functions uses
`ext_of_forall_integral_eq_of_IsFiniteMeasure` (*not* the weak topology). This is the same lemma
Tool 2 needs, so if the campaign builds it once it is available everywhere.

**Recommendation:** defer. The campaign needs the direction "unique ergodicity ⟹ uniform", not
its converse, and every line of the converse is a line not spent on Tool 2.

## II.3.3 Blueprint 2

Tool 2: the same for an interval exchange whose only invariant probability measure is Lebesgue's,
which is not continuous — the split interval, its germs, the transfer of measures, and the plan of
the twelve modules.

# Blueprint 2 — interval exchanges: uniform Birkhoff convergence from unique ergodicity

**Tool 2.** Let `T` be an interval exchange of `[0,1)` whose only invariant probability measure
carried by `[0,1)` is Lebesgue's. Then the Birkhoff averages of every continuous function converge
to their integral **uniformly on `[0,1)`**. `T` is not continuous, so Tool 1 does not apply to it
directly.

**Source.** J.-C. Yoccoz, *Interval exchange maps and translation surfaces*, top of p. 55
(pp. 68 of the PDF):

> A slightly better answer is obtained by using that, by the same theorem of Masur and Veech,
> almost all `T` are actually uniquely ergodic. Indeed, if `f` is a uniquely ergodic minimal
> homeomorphism of a compact metric space `X` and `φ` is a continuous function on `X`, the
> convergence of the Birkhoff sums of `φ` holds for any initial value `x₀` and is uniform in `x₀`.
> Here, `T` is not a homeomorphism and the characteristic function of `I^t_α` is not continuous
> but this is not a problem in reason of the following trick.
>
> Split any point in the forward orbit of the singularities of `T⁻¹` and the backward orbit of the
> singularities of `T` into its left and right limit. One obtains, equipped with the order
> topology, a compact metric space `Ĩ`. The i.e.m `T` induces on `Ĩ` a homeomorphism `T̃` which is
> easily seen to be uniquely ergodic when `T` is. Also, the interval `I^t_α` corresponds to a
> clopen set in `Ĩ` so its characteristic function is continuous.

The paragraph is a correct sketch of a correct proof after **three repairs**, recorded in §8:
the space must be the interval with only the **interior** singularities doubled (`X° = [a+, b−]`; if
the two endpoints are doubled as well, one adds two isolated fixed points of `T̃`, §2.7);
`T̃` is a homeomorphism only in the germ sense, and `p ∘ T̃ = T ∘ p` holds on right germs only
(§8.1); and the transfer of unique ergodicity is not "easy": it goes through the defect identity of
§4.2 and through (H2), which is *not* an extra hypothesis — it follows from unique ergodicity itself
by the six-line "periodic interval" argument of §4.4. The source's own route to (H2) (unique
ergodicity ⇒ minimality ⇒ no connection) is not available, because Keane's "no connection ⇒
minimal" is not an equivalence for `d ≥ 3`: see §8.6.

§1 fixes notation and the elementary facts about the one-sided limits of an interval exchange.
§2 is the compact space, §3 the homeomorphism, §4 the transfer of invariant measures, §5 the
theorem, §6 the a.e. hypothesis, §7 the passage to `MasurVeechFun`, §8 the gap report, §9 the Lean
specification, §10 traps, §11 milestones.

---

## 1. Setting, notation, and the one-sided limits of an interval exchange

### 1.1 The datum

Fix reals `a < b`. An **interval exchange on `[a,b)`** is a bijection `T : ℝ → ℝ` with

  (I1) `T x = x` for `x ∉ [a,b)`  (in particular `T b = b`);
  (I2) `T '' [a,b) = [a,b)`;
  (I3) `IsCutSet T a b s` for some finite set `s ⊆ [a,b)` with `a ∈ s` (`CutSet.lean`).

`IsCutSet` says exactly: `T` is a translation on every cell `[c_i, c_{i+1})` of the partition of
`[a,b)` by `s = {c_0 = a < c_1 < … < c_{d−1}}`, and the cells tile `[a,b)`
(`IsCutSet.cells_union`). The relevant API already exists: `IsCutSet.cellLeft`, `cellStarts`,
`cellPos`, `cellLen`, `cells_union`, `cells_disjoint`, `image_cell`, `image_cell_disjoint`,
`image_cells_union`, `map_of_mem_cell`, `measurable`, `measure_preimage`.

In the application `a = 0`, `b = 1`, `T = mkIETFun lam π 0` on the simplex and `s = mkIETCuts lam 0 1`
(`isCutSet_mkIETCuts`); the hypothesis `∑ lam = 1` is what makes (I2) hold.

### 1.2 Two-sided limits

**Definition 1.1 (left limit).** For `x ∈ (a,b]` let `c(x) := max {c ∈ s : c < x}` (nonempty since
`a ∈ s` and `a < x`) and put

  `L x := x + (T (c x) − c x)`.

Put `L a := a`. (So `L` is defined on `[a,b]`; we do not care about it elsewhere and extend it by
`L x = x` off `[a,b]` if a total function is wanted.)

**Lemma 1.2.** (i) `L x ∈ [a,b]` for `x ∈ [a,b]`.
(ii) `Tendsto T (𝓝[<] x) (𝓝 (L x))` for `x ∈ (a,b]`, and `Tendsto T (𝓝[<] a) (𝓝 a)` (from outside
the interval `T` is the identity, so the left limit at `a` is `a = L a`).
(iii) `Tendsto T (𝓝[>] x) (𝓝 (T x))` for every `x ∈ [a,b)` ("**the value is the right limit**").
(iv) `L x = T x` for every `x ∈ [a,b) ∖ s`; at `x = b` this can fail (`L b = b + δ_{d−1}` against
`T b = b`), and then `b ∈ J`, consistently with `J ⊆ s ∪ {b}` below.

*Proof.* (i) If `x = a`, `L x = a`. If `a < x`, `c := c(x) ∈ s` and `T c ∈ [a,b)` (the image of a cut
under `T` is the left end of the image of the cell on its right, so lies in `[a,b)`); hence
`L x = c + (T c − c) + (x − c) = T c + (x − c) ∈ [a,b)` because `c < x` and `T c < b`.
(ii) For `y ∈ (c(x), x)` one has `¬ Separated s y x` (no cut lies in `(y,x]`), so
`T y − y = T (c x) − (c x)` by `IsCutSet.transl_of_not_separated`; let `y ↑ x`.
(iii) For `y ∈ (x, c')` with `c'` the next cut (or `b`) the same identity holds with `c(x) = x`'s own
cell, and `T y → x + (T x − x) = T x`. Note that `T x = x + (T (cellLeft x) − cellLeft x)` by the same
lemma applied to the pair `(cellLeft x, x)`, which are not separated. (iv) At `x ∉ s` the cut
`c(x)` and `x` are not separated, so `L x = x + (T (c x) − c x) = T x` by the same identity; and
`T` is continuous at `x` exactly when the two one-sided limits and the value agree, i.e. when
`x ∉ J`. ∎

**Lemma 1.3.** `T⁻¹` is an interval exchange on `[a,b)`: it is a translation on each cell of the
partition of `[a,b)` by the finite set `s'` of left endpoints of the intervals `T '' [c_i, c_{i+1})`,
i.e. `IsCutSet T⁻¹ a b s'`, and it satisfies (I1)–(I3). Explicitly, for `T = mkIETFun lam π a` one
has `T⁻¹ = mkIETFun (imageLengths π lam) π.symm a` (`mkIETFun_inv_left`) with the cut set
`mkIETCuts (imageLengths π lam) a t` (`isCutSet_mkIETCuts`).

*Proof.* `T` is a translation on the cell `[c_i, c_{i+1})`, so `T⁻¹` is a translation on the image
interval `T '' [c_i, c_{i+1}) =: [u_i, v_i)`; the `[u_i, v_i)` tile `[a,b)`
(`Equiv.IsIET.image_cells_union` — the statement is about `IET` but only uses `IsCutSet`), and
`u_i ∈ [a,b)`. Apply `IsCutSet` with `s' := {u_i}`. ∎

**Definition 1.4 (the jump set).** `J := {x ∈ [a,b] : L x ≠ T x}`.

**Lemma 1.5.** `J` is finite, `J ⊆ s ∪ {b}`, and `J` is exactly the discontinuity set of `T` on
`[a,b]`. Similarly the jump set `J'` of `T⁻¹` is finite and `⊆ s' ∪ {b}`.

*Proof.* `L x ≠ T x` can only happen at a cut (`L x = T x` off `s` by Lemma 1.2(iv)) or at `b`
(where `L b` is the right end of the last image cell, `T b = b`). ∎

### 1.3 The split set and the left-limit dynamics

**Definition 1.6.** `D := ⋃_{n ∈ ℤ} T^n '' (s ∪ s' ∪ {b}) ⊆ [a,b]`.

**Lemma 1.7.** (i) `D` is countable and `s ∪ s' ∪ {b} ⊆ D`.
(ii) `T '' D = D` (so `T^n '' D = D` for all `n ∈ ℤ`).
(iii) `L '' D ⊆ D`.
(iv) For every `n ∈ ℕ`, the discontinuity set of `T^n` is contained in `D`, and likewise for `T^{-n}`.

*Proof.* (i),(ii) are immediate (`T` is a bijection and `D` is a union of full orbits).
(iii) For `x ∈ D`: if `x ∉ J` then `L x = T x ∈ D`; if `x ∈ J` then `x ∈ s ∪ {b}`, and then
`L x` is the right end of the image of a cell, which is either `b` or a left end of an image cell,
i.e. `L x ∈ s' ∪ {b} ⊆ D`. (Careful: this covers `x ∈ s`; for `x = b ∈ J`, `L b` is the right end of
the last image cell, again in `s' ∪ {b}`.) (iv) `T^n` is discontinuous at `x` iff `T` is
discontinuous at `T^{n−1} x` iff `T^{n−1} x ∈ s`, iff `x ∈ T^{-(n−1)} '' s ⊆ D`. ∎

**Lemma 1.8 (elementary structure of `L`).** Let `s = {c_0 = a < c_1 < … < c_{d−1}}`, let
`δ_i := T(c_i) − c_i` be the displacement of the cell `[c_i, c_{i+1})` (with `c_d := b`), and let
`u_i := T(c_i) = c_i + δ_i`, so that the image cells `[u_i, u_i + (c_{i+1} − c_i))` tile `[a,b)`.
Then:

(i) for `x ∈ (c_i, c_{i+1}]` one has `L x = x + δ_i`, and `T x = x + δ_i` for `x ∈ [c_i, c_{i+1})`;
(ii) **if `T` is injective** (`IsCutSet` alone does not give this — see the remark), `L` maps
`(c_i, c_{i+1}]` bijectively onto `(u_i, u_i + (c_{i+1} − c_i)]`, and these `d`
intervals tile `(a,b]`; together with `L a = a` this makes `L` a bijection of `[a,b]`;
(iii) on the open cell `(c_i, c_{i+1})` both `T` and `L` are the *increasing* translation
`y ↦ y + δ_i`; `T(c_i) = c_i + δ_i`; and `T x = L x` exactly at the points `x` at which `T` is
continuous (i.e. off `J`);
(iv) `L` is continuous on each `(c_i, c_{i+1})` and left continuous at every `c_{i+1}` (and at `a`
in the sense `L|_[a,b]` with `L a = a`); its discontinuity set is contained in `s`.

*Proof.* (i) For `x ∈ (c_i, c_{i+1})`: the largest cut below `x` is `c_i`, and `x`, `c_i` are not
separated, so `T x − x = T c_i − c_i = δ_i` (`IsCutSet.transl_of_not_separated`); and
`L x = x + (T c_i − c_i)` by Definition 1.1 (for `x = c_{i+1}` the same computation with the pair
`(c_i, c_{i+1})`, which are not separated, gives the left-hand formula; for `T` at `x = c_i` the
same identity applied to the pair `(c_i, c_i)` gives `T c_i = c_i + δ_i`).
(ii) By (i), `L|_(c_i,c_{i+1}]` is the translation
`y ↦ y + δ_i`, so its image is `(c_i + δ_i, c_{i+1} + δ_i] = (u_i, u_i + (c_{i+1} − c_i)]`; if `T` is
injective the image cells tile `[a,b)`, i.e. `[u_i, u_i + (c_{i+1} − c_i))` are disjoint with union
`[a,b)` (`Equiv.IsIET.image_cells_union`), so their right-open/right-closed variants tile `(a,b)`
and adding `a ↦ a` gives a bijection of `[a,b]`. (iii) is (i), plus `L x = T x ⟺ x ∉ J` (Lemma 1.5).
(iv) On `(c_i, c_{i+1})` the map is a translation; at `c_{i+1}` (from inside)
`L y = y + δ_i → c_{i+1} + δ_i = L c_{i+1}` by (i). ∎

**Remark 1.9 (two corrections found in formalisation; the Lean `Limits.lean` carries them).**
`IsCutSet` alone is weaker than an exchange, in two ways that matter for `L` and must not be
forgotten:

* at `x = b` one has `L b = b + δ_{d−1}`, which differs from `T b = b` whenever the last cell is not
  translated by `0` — even though `b ∉ s`. So "`L = T` off the cuts" must be read at `x ∈ [a,b)`;
  at `b` the discrepancy is recorded in `J` (which is why `J ⊆ s ∪ {b}`).
* `L` need not be injective when `T` is only assumed to satisfy `IsCutSet` (counterexample: `a = 0`,
  `b = 2`, `s = {0,1}`, `T x = x` on `[0,1)` and `T x = x − 1/2` on `[1,2)`: then `T` is not
  injective and `L (3/4) = L (5/4) = 3/4`). For an `Equiv` — in particular for
  `T = mkIETFun lam π a` — injectivity holds (`Equiv.injective`) and so does (ii).

With Lemma 1.8 the two-sided limits collected in Lemma 1.2 are the only analytic input needed for
the whole construction; in particular `L` is a bijection of `[a,b]` (used for the injectivity of `T̃`
in Lemma 3.4), and `T`, `L` are increasing translations on each closed-left cell (used for the
continuity of `T̃` in Lemma 3.3).

**Notation (H2) — no periodic left limit.** For no `x ∈ (a,b]` and `k ≥ 1` is `L^[k] x = x`.
`L a = a` always, so `a` must be excluded.

This is **not a hypothesis**: §4.4 proves it from unique ergodicity, by an elementary "periodic
interval" argument. It is stated separately because it is exactly the property of `L` that the
transfer theorem of §4.2 needs, and because it is *sharp*: §8.3 shows that a periodic left limit
does destroy the conclusion. (The source's route — unique ergodicity ⇒ minimality ⇒ no connection
⇒ … — is *not* available: "no connection" is not equivalent to minimality, see §8.6.)

---

## 2. The split space

### 2.1 Definition

Throughout, `D ⊆ ℝ` is the countable set of Definition 1.6. For `d : D` we write `(d : ℝ)` for its
coercion.

```lean
/-- The set of split points. -/
def splitSet (T : IET a b) : Set ℝ := ⋃ n : ℤ, T^[n] '' (s ∪ s' ∪ {b})
```

**Definition 2.1.** `X` is the set of pairs `z = (x, χ)` with `x ∈ [a,b]`, `χ : D → Bool`, and

  `(x < d → χ d = false)` and `(d < x → χ d = true)` for every `d : D`.

Intuitively `χ d` records on which side of the split point `d` the point sits (`false` = left,
`true` = right), and at `x = d` the value `χ d` is free — that is exactly the doubling.

```lean
def SplitI (a b : ℝ) (D : Set ℝ) : Type :=
  {z : ℝ × (D → Bool) // z.1 ∈ Set.Icc a b ∧
    ∀ d : D, (z.1 < (d : ℝ) → z.2 d = false) ∧ ((d : ℝ) < z.1 → z.2 d = true)}
```

We give `X` the subspace topology of `ℝ × (D → Bool)` (on `D → Bool` the product topology, `Bool`
discrete).

**Lemma 2.2 (topology).** `X` is a nonempty compact Hausdorff pseudo-metrizable Borel space.

*Proof.* `X` is closed in `[a,b] × (D → Bool)`: each defining condition is a finite union of closed
sets (`{x < d} ∪ {χ d = false}` and `{d < x} ∪ {χ d = true}`), and `D` is countable so the
intersection is countable. `[a,b]` is compact, `D → Bool` is compact (`Pi.compactSpace`, Tychonoff
for the discrete two-point space), so the product is compact and the closed subset too.
Hausdorff: subspace of a Hausdorff space. Pseudo-metrizable: `PseudoMetrizableSpace.subtype` and
`pseudoMetrizableSpace_pi` (`Topology/Metrizable/Basic.lean`), all factors being pseudo-metrizable.
Borel: `Subtype.borelSpace`, `Prod.borelSpace` (needs `SecondCountableTopologyEither`, available
from `SecondCountableTopology ℝ`) and `Pi.borelSpace` (needs `[Countable D]` and second countable
factors: `D` countable because `D.Countable`, `Bool` finite). Nonempty: it contains `rightGerm a`
(2.3). ∎

**Remark 2.3 (this topology is the order topology).** Ordering `X` by
`(x,χ) < (y,χ') ⟺ x < y ∨ (x = y ∧ χ x = false ∧ χ' x = true)` (with the evident convention at
`x ∉ D`) makes `X` a linear order whose order topology is the subspace topology above: the rays
`{z : z ≥ rightGerm d} = {z : χ d = true}` and `{z : z ≤ leftGerm d} = {z : χ d = false}` are
clopen, and `{z : x(z) ∈ U}` is open. This remark is the bridge to the source's "order topology";
the formalisation should use the product description, which makes compactness and continuity
immediate, and never mention the order.

### 2.2 Projection, the two sections, and the fibres

```lean
/-- The projection to `[a,b]`; it collapses the two germs of a split point. -/
def proj : SplitI a b D → ℝ := fun z => z.1.1

/-- The right germ of `x`. -/
def rightGerm (x : ℝ) (hx : x ∈ Set.Icc a b) : SplitI a b D :=
  ⟨(x, fun d => decide ((d : ℝ) ≤ x)), …, …⟩

/-- The left germ of `x`. -/
def leftGerm (x : ℝ) (hx : x ∈ Set.Icc a b) : SplitI a b D :=
  ⟨(x, fun d => decide ((d : ℝ) < x)), …, …⟩
```

**Lemma 2.4.** (i) `proj` is continuous; `proj '' X = [a,b]`.
(ii) `proj (rightGerm x) = x = proj (leftGerm x)`.
(iii) If `x ∉ D` then `rightGerm x = leftGerm x`.
(iv) If `x ∈ D` then `rightGerm x ≠ leftGerm x` and every `z ∈ X` with `proj z = x` is one of the
two.
(v) **One-sided convergence.** For `x ∈ [a,b]`: `rightGerm y → leftGerm x` as `y ↑ x` (i.e.
`Tendsto rightGerm (𝓝[<] x) (𝓝 (leftGerm x))`, as soon as the germs are taken along `y ∈ [a,b)`),
and `Tendsto rightGerm (𝓝[>] x) (𝓝 (rightGerm x))`. Dually for `leftGerm`.
(vi) **The right-germ section has exactly two missing points.** With `I° := [a,b)` and
`X° := closure (rightGerm '' I°)`, one has
`X° = X ∖ {leftGerm a, rightGerm b}`. Both deleted points are isolated in `X` (nothing lies strictly
below `leftGerm a`, nothing strictly above `rightGerm b`), and they are exactly the two points of
`X` that no sequence of right germs of `[a,b)` can reach. Moreover `X°` is closed in `X`, hence
compact, and `rightGerm y ∈ X°` for every `y ∈ [a,b)`. Consequently, for every `z ∈ X°` and every
neighbourhood `U` of `z` there is `y ∈ [a,b)` with `rightGerm y ∈ U`: if `z = rightGerm x` take
`y = x`; if `z = leftGerm x` with `x > a` take `y ↑ x`.

*Proof.* (i),(ii),(iii) are the definitions. (iv) two points with the same first coordinate differ
only in `χ (x)`; the constraints determine `χ d` for `d ≠ x`, and `χ x` is free, giving exactly two
points. (v) both coordinates converge: the first because `y → x`, the second because for each
`d : D` the value `decide (d ≤ y)` is eventually `decide (d ≤ x)` (if `d < x`) or `decide (d < y)`
is eventually `false` (if `d > x`), and the two sections agree at `d = x`. (vi) `rightGerm a ∈ X°`
(take `y = a`), and for `x > a`, `rightGerm y → leftGerm x` as `y ↑ x` (v), so every `leftGerm x`
with `x > a` is in `X°`; `leftGerm a` is not (it is the strict minimum of `X` and `rightGerm y ≥
rightGerm a > leftGerm a`), and `rightGerm b` is not (`rightGerm y → leftGerm b` as `y ↑ b`, and
`leftGerm b ≠ rightGerm b` because `b ∈ D`). Conversely every point of `X ∖ {leftGerm a, rightGerm b}`
is `rightGerm x` (take `y = x`) or `leftGerm x` with `x > a`. ∎

**Corollary 2.6.** `T̃` maps `X°` into `X°`.**

*Proof.* `T̃` is injective (Lemma 3.4 below) and `T̃ (leftGerm a) = leftGerm a`, `T̃ (rightGerm b) =
rightGerm b` (`L a = a`, `T b = b`). So the two deleted points have no other preimages. ∎

**Remark 2.7 (do not double the endpoints).** The two deleted points are *not* part of the dynamics:
they are the two "one-sided" germs of the endpoints of the interval, which are never approached from
inside `[a,b)`, and `T̃` fixes them. Keeping them (i.e. splitting `a` and `b` as well) adds two
isolated fixed points and destroys unique ergodicity of `T̃` — see §4.5 and §8.2. The right object,
and the one the source means, is the interval with only the **interior** singularities split, i.e.
`X° = [a+, b−]`.

### 2.3 The "one-sided" neighbourhoods

Two families of open sets are used constantly below; both are open for the trivial reason that they
are described by one coordinate and one inequality:

  `U⁺ x := {z : x < proj z} ∪ {z : proj z = x ∧ (z = rightGerm x)}`  ("strictly to the right of `x`"),
  `U⁻ x := {z : proj z < x} ∪ {z : proj z = x ∧ (z = leftGerm x)}`.

**Lemma 2.5.** (i) `U⁺ x` and `U⁻ x` are open, and `U⁺ x = {z : (χ z) ⟨x, _⟩ = true}` when `x ∈ D`
(so `U⁺ x` is even clopen); `U⁻ x` similarly.
(ii) If `z ∈ U⁺ x` then `proj z ≥ x`, with equality only for `z = rightGerm x`.
(iii) `U⁺ x` is a neighbourhood of `rightGerm x`, `U⁻ x` of `leftGerm x`.

*Proof.* `{χ · d = true}` is open (one coordinate), and `{x < proj ·}` is open; their union is the
set displayed. Then (ii),(iii) are immediate. ∎

---

## 3. The germ map `T̃`

### 3.1 Definition

For `z = (x, χ) ∈ X` put `side z := χ ⟨x, h⟩` if `h : x ∈ D`, and `side z := true` if `x ∉ D` (the
choice is immaterial there). Define

  `x'(z) := if x ∈ D ∧ side z = false then L x else T x`,
  `χ'(z) d := decide (x'(z) > (d:ℝ) ∨ (x'(z) = (d:ℝ) ∧ side z = true))`,
  `T̃ z := (x'(z), χ'(z))`.

So the right germ of `x` is sent to the right germ of `T x`, and the left germ of `x` is sent to
the left germ of `L x`. That asymmetry is forced by Lemma 1.2(iii) and cannot be removed: **there
is no homeomorphism of any compactification of `[a,b)` that covers `T` and satisfies
`p ∘ T̃ = T ∘ p` at the left germs of the cuts** (take a net `y ↑ c` at a cut `c`).

**Lemma 3.1 (`T̃` lands in `X`).** `T̃ z ∈ X`.

*Proof.* `x'(z) ∈ [a,b]`: `T` maps `[a,b)` into `[a,b)` and fixes `b`; `L` maps `[a,b]` into `[a,b]`
(Lemma 1.2(i)). The constraints on `χ'` hold by construction of the `decide`. Note `x'(z) ∈ D`
whenever `x(z) ∈ D` (either `T x` or `L x`, both in `D` by Lemma 1.7(ii),(iii)), so the assignment
is consistent. ∎

### 3.2 The three structural lemmas

**Lemma 3.2 (semi-conjugacy on right germs).** `T̃ (rightGerm x) = rightGerm (T x)` for
`x ∈ [a,b]`. Consequently `T̃^[n] (rightGerm x) = rightGerm (T^[n] x)` and
`proj (T̃^[n] (rightGerm x)) = T^[n] x` for all `n`.

*Proof.* At `x`: `side = true` (for `x ∉ D`, by convention; for `x ∈ D`, `χ x = decide (x ≤ x) = true`),
so `x' = T x`; and `χ'(rightGerm (Tx)) d = decide (Tx > d ∨ (Tx = d ∧ true)) = decide (d ≤ Tx)` by
the constraints (for `d ≠ Tx` the two forms agree; for `d = Tx` both give `true`). ∎

**Lemma 3.3 (`T̃` is continuous).** `T̃ : X → X` is continuous.

*Proof.* Continuity into a subspace of a product is coordinatewise.

*(a) `z ↦ x'(z)` is continuous.* Let `z ∈ X`, `x := proj z`.
 — If `x ∉ D`: for `z' → z` we have `proj z' → x`, and `x'(z')` is either `T (proj z')` or
   `L (proj z')`. The first tends to `T x` by Lemma 1.2(iii); the second tends to `L x = T x`
   because `x ∉ D ⊇ J` (Lemma 1.5) and `L` is continuous at points off `J` (Lemma 1.2(ii) plus
   `L = T` off `J`). Pass to the limit along the net: `x'(z') → T x = x'(z)`.
 — If `z = rightGerm x`, `x ∈ D`: by Lemma 2.5(ii) every `z'` near `z` has `proj z' ≥ x`, so
   `proj z' ∈ [x, x+δ)`; the branches `T (proj z')` and `L (proj z')` both tend to `T x`: the first
   by right continuity (Lemma 1.2(iii)), the second because for `proj z' > x` close to `x` we have
   `proj z' ∉ J` (as `J` is finite and in particular has a gap above `x` unless `x` is its maximum;
   in that case use `x' = T (proj z')`), whence `L (proj z') = T (proj z') → T x`.
 — If `z = leftGerm x`, `x ∈ D`: every `z'` near `z` has `proj z' ≤ x`, and `x'(z') ∈ {T y, L y}`
   with `y := proj z' ↑ x`; both tend to `L x`: `T y → L x` is Lemma 1.2(ii), and `L y → L x` is the
   left continuity of `L`, Lemma 1.8(iv).

*(b) For each `d : D`, `z ↦ χ'(z) d` is continuous.* Let `z`, `x' := x'(z)`. If `x' > d`, then
`x'(z') > d` for `z'` near `z` (continuity of `x'`), so `χ' z' d = true = χ' z d`. If `x' < d`,
likewise `false`. If `x' = d`: then in particular `d = x'(z) ∈ [a,b]`, and
`χ'(z) d = (side z = true)`.
 — If `side z = true`: for `z'` near `z` we have `x'(z') ≥ x'(z) = d`, with equality only at `z' = z`
   itself or at the single (different) point `leftGerm x` when `x ∈ D`, which is excluded
   eventually because `X` is Hausdorff. More precisely, `x'` is *non-decreasing across right
   germs*: for `z'` near `rightGerm x` with `proj z' > x` one has `x'(z') ≥ T x`, because either
   branch is the increasing translation `y ↦ y + δ_i` on the cell of `x` (Lemma 1.8(iii)), so that
   `x'(z') = T x + (y − x) ≥ T x`. Hence eventually `x'(z') > d` or `x'(z') = d` with
   `side z' = true`, and `χ' z' d = true` in both cases.
 — If `side z = false`: dually, `x'(z') ≤ d` eventually and equality forces `side z' = false`.

So `χ'(·) d` is continuous. ∎

**Lemma 3.4 (`T̃` is a bijection).** `T̃` is injective and surjective; its inverse is the germ map
of `T⁻¹` (Definition 3.1 applied to `T⁻¹`, whose jump set is `J'`).

*Proof.* *Injective.* Let `z ≠ z'`. If `side z = side z'`, then `x'(z) ≠ x'(z')` (both branches `T`
and `L` are injective on their sides: `T` is a bijection of `[a,b)`, and `L` is a bijection of `[a,b]`
by Lemma 1.8(ii)). If `side z ≠ side z'`: then
`z = rightGerm x`, `z' = leftGerm x` with `x ∈ D`; `x'(z) = T x`, `x'(z') = L x`, and
`T x ≠ L x` because `x ∈ D` and `D ⊇ s` covers all the continuity points off which `T` and `L`
differ (Lemma 1.5).
*Surjective.* For `w ∈ X` with `proj w = y`, consider `y' := T⁻¹ y` and
`y'' := L⁻¹ y` (both exist, `T`, `L` being bijections); at least one of the two candidate preimages
exists in `X` by the same case analysis;
equivalently, exhibit the inverse map: the germ map of `T⁻¹`, and check
`germMap (T⁻¹) ∘ germMap T = id` and the reverse, on right and left germs separately. For right
germs this is immediate; for left germs use `L (L⁻¹ y) = y` and `L⁻¹ (L y) = y` (Lemma 1.8(ii)). ∎

Lemma 3.4 is the least pleasant part; the campaign only needs **injectivity** (see §4.2), so if the
bijection proof is expensive, state `T̃_injective` alone and prove it by the case analysis (the
inverse map can be deferred).

**Lemma 3.5 (`T̃` preserves sides).** `side (T̃ z) = side z`, and
`proj (T̃ z) = T (proj z)` for `z = rightGerm x`, `proj (T̃ z) = L (proj z)` for `z = leftGerm x`.

---

## 4. Invariant measures on `X`

Throughout this section `λ` denotes Lebesgue measure restricted to `[a,b)` (a probability:
`λ := volume.restrict (Set.Ico a b)`), extended by `0` to all of `ℝ`. It is atomless and
`λ D = 0` because `D` is countable. `ν` is a probability measure on `X`.

### 4.1 The lift of an atomless measure is unique

**Lemma 4.1 (lifting lemma).** Let `s : [a,b] → X` be a Borel section of `proj` (`proj (s x) = x`).
If `ν` is a probability on `X` with `proj_* ν = λ`, then `ν = s_* λ`.

*Proof.* Since `λ` is atomless and `proj_*ν = λ`, every point has `ν`-measure zero:
`ν {z} ≤ ν (proj ⁻¹' {proj z}) = λ {proj z} = 0`; in particular `ν (proj ⁻¹' D) = 0` because `D` is
countable (a countable union of sets of measure zero).
Now let `A ⊆ X` be Borel and put `E := proj '' A`, `A₀ := A ∖ proj ⁻¹' D`. On `proj ⁻¹' ([a,b] ∖ D)`
the map `proj` is injective, hence
`A₀ = proj ⁻¹' (E ∖ D)`: the inclusion `⊆` is immediate, and if `z ∉ D` has `proj z = proj a` for
some `a ∈ A₀` then `a` is not split either (its projection is not in `D`) and injectivity gives
`z = a ∈ A₀`. Therefore `ν A = ν A₀ = λ (E ∖ D) = λ E`.
For `s_*λ` the same computation gives `s_*λ A = λ (s ⁻¹' A)` and
`s ⁻¹' A ∖ D = E ∖ D` (again by injectivity of `proj` off `D`, since `proj (s y) = y`), so
`s_*λ A = λ E`. Hence `ν = s_*λ`.
The step from a single Borel set to all Borel sets is *not* an application of the computation to a
general `A` (for which `proj '' A` need not be Borel); it is the standard criterion "two finite
measures agreeing on a π-system generating the σ-algebra agree". The π-system is the family

  `{z : proj z ∈ (q₁, q₂)} ∩ {z : χ d₁ = ε₁} ∩ … ∩ {z : χ d_k = ε_k}`,  `q_i ∈ ℚ`, `d_i : D`, `k ∈ ℕ`,

which generates `Borel X` (it contains the open intervals in the first coordinate and every
coordinate set `{χ d = ε}`), is closed under finite intersections, and covers `X` already with the
single member `k = 0, (q₁,q₂) = (a−1, b+1)`. For such a set, `proj '' A` is
`(q₁,q₂) ∩ ⋂_i (if ε_i = true then [d_i, b] else [a, d_i])`, *explicitly* Borel, so the computation
above applies verbatim; conclude with `MeasureTheory.Measure.ext_of_isPiSystem` (or
`ext_of_generate_finite`). Measurability of `s` (needed for `s_*λ`) is `Measurable.subtype_mk`
from the two coordinates `x ↦ x` and `x ↦ decide (d ≤ x)`. ∎

**Corollary 4.2.** Any two probabilities `ν₁, ν₂` on `X` with `proj_*ν₁ = proj_*ν₂ = λ` are equal.

### 4.2 The defect identity

**Lemma 4.3 (mass is constant along the orbit).** If `ν` is `T̃`-invariant then
`ν {T̃ z} = ν {z}` for every `z ∈ X` (invariance gives `ν A = ν (T̃ ⁻¹' A)`; apply it to
`A = {T̃ z}` and use injectivity of `T̃`, Lemma 3.4).

**Lemma 4.4 (defect identity).** Let `ν` be a `T̃`-invariant probability and `ρ := proj_* ν`. Then
for every bounded continuous `g : ℝ → ℝ`,

  `∫ g dρ − ∫ g d(T_* ρ) = Σ_{c ∈ J} ν {leftGerm c} · (g (L c) − g (T c))`.

*Proof.* `proj (T̃ z) = L (proj z)` for `z = leftGerm c`, `c ∈ J`, and `= T (proj z)` in every other
case (Lemma 3.5): for `z = leftGerm c` with `c ∉ J` the two values agree; for `z = rightGerm c`
the value is `T c`; for `proj z ∉ D` there is a single germ and `T = L` there. Hence
`∫ g d(proj_*(T̃_* ν)) = ∫ g (L (proj z)) dν(z)` restricted to the finite set of `leftGerm c`,
`c ∈ J`, plus `∫ g (T (proj z)) dν` elsewhere. Since `ν` is `T̃`-invariant,
`proj_*(T̃_*ν) = proj_*ν = ρ`. Subtract `∫ g d(T_*ρ) = ∫ g (T (proj z)) dν(z)`. ∎

**Lemma 4.5 (the defect vanishes).** Assume (H2). Let `ν` be a `T̃`-invariant probability on `X`
with `ν X° = 1`, where `X° := closure (rightGerm '' [a,b))` (Lemma 2.4(vi)). Then
`ν {leftGerm c} = 0` for every `c ∈ J`.

*Proof.* (i) For `c ∈ J ∩ (a,b]`: if `ν {leftGerm c} > 0` then, by Lemma 4.3, `ν` gives the same
positive mass to every point of the `T̃`-orbit of `leftGerm c`, whose projections are
`c, L c, L^[2] c, …` (Lemma 3.5); by (H2) that orbit is infinite, and the masses would sum to more
than `1`. (ii) For `c = a`: `leftGerm a ∉ X°` (Lemma 2.4(vi)), so `ν {leftGerm a} = 0` because
`ν X° = 1` and `X°` is closed. ∎

**Theorem 4.6 (transfer of invariance).** Assume (H2), let `ν` be a `T̃`-invariant probability on
`X` with `ν X° = 1`. Then `proj_* ν = λ`.

*Proof.* By Lemma 4.5 all the coefficients in Lemma 4.4 vanish, so `T_*ρ = ρ` for
`ρ := proj_*ν`: `ρ` is a `T`-invariant probability on `[a,b]`. Moreover `ρ {b} = 0`: the fibre over
`b` is `{leftGerm b, rightGerm b}`, `rightGerm b ∉ X°` (Lemma 2.4(vi)), and `ν {leftGerm b} = 0` by
(H2) and Lemma 4.3 as in 4.5(i) (take `x = b` in (H2)). Hence `ρ` is carried by `[a,b)` and is
therefore an invariant probability measure with total mass `1` on `[a,b)`, so `ρ = λ` by the
uniqueness hypothesis (H1). ∎

**Corollary 4.7.** Under (H2), `ν = rightGerm_* λ` for every `T̃`-invariant probability on `X` with
`ν X° = 1` (combine 4.6 with Lemma 4.1, using that `rightGerm` is a Borel section and `λ {b} = 0`).

### 4.3 Existence

**Lemma 4.8.** `rightGerm_* λ` is `T̃`-invariant.

*Proof.* `T̃_* (rightGerm_*λ) = (T̃ ∘ rightGerm)_* λ = (rightGerm ∘ T)_* λ = rightGerm_* (T_*λ) =
rightGerm_*λ`, using Lemma 3.2 and the invariance of `λ` under `T`
(`Assembly.invariant_unitMeas` / `Equiv.IsIET.measure_preimage`). ∎

So `X` always carries at least one invariant probability measure, namely the lift of `λ`; and
Corollary 4.7 says that under (H2) it is the only invariant measure supported on `X°`, i.e. that
`T̃|_{X°}` is uniquely ergodic (§4.5). This is the correct reading of the source's "`T̃` is uniquely
ergodic".

### 4.4 (H2) follows from unique ergodicity: a periodic left limit is a periodic interval

**Lemma 4.9.** Let `T` be an interval exchange on `[a,b)` in the sense of §1.1, let `x₀ ∈ (a,b]` and
`k ≥ 1` with `L^[k] x₀ = x₀`. Then there is `ε > 0` such that,
putting `x_i := L^[i] x₀` and `J_i := (x_i − ε, x_i)` for `i = 0, …, k−1`,

  `T '' J_i = J_{i+1}`  (indices mod `k`),  in particular `T '' K = K` for `K := ⋃_{i<k} J_i`,

and moreover `T^[k]` is the identity on `J_0`. Consequently `λ|_K` is a `T`-invariant finite
measure with `0 < λ(K) ≤ kε`, and `λ|_K / λ(K)` is a `T`-invariant probability measure on `[a,b)`.

*Proof.* For `i < k` let `c_i` be the largest cut below `x_i` (it exists since `x_i > a`: if some
`x_i = a` then `L a = a` forces the whole cycle to be `{a}`, contrary to `x₀ > a`), and put
`ε := min_i (x_i − c_i) > 0`. Then `J_i = (x_i − ε, x_i) ⊆ (c_i, x_i]` contains no cut, so `T` is
a translation on `J_i`, say by `δ_i` (`IsCutSet.transl_of_not_separated`). By the explicit formula
of Definition 1.1, `x_i + δ_i = L x_i = x_{i+1}`. Hence `T '' J_i = (x_i + δ_i − ε, x_i + δ_i) =
J_{i+1}` (indices mod `k`), and in particular `T '' J_{k−1} = J_0`, so `T` permutes the `J_i`
cyclically. Each `T|_{J_i}` is a translation, hence preserves Lebesgue measure, so `λ|_K` is
`T`-invariant; and `λ(K) ≤ kε < 1` for `ε < 1/k`. Finally `T^[k]` is a translation of `J_0` onto
itself, hence the identity. (Note that `λ|_K` is *not* `λ` when `λ(K) < 1`: `ν := λ|_K/λ(K)`
satisfies `ν(K) = 1 > λ(K)`.) ∎

**Sharper form (as formalised in `Limits.lean`).** One does not need the invariant *Lebesgue*
measure on `K = ⋃_i J_i`: any point `y ∈ J_0 = (x₀ − ε, x₀)` satisfies `T^[k] y = y`, because
`T^[k]` is a translation of `J_0` onto itself, hence the identity. So a periodic left limit already
produces a genuine **periodic point** of `T`, and the atomic measure `k⁻¹ Σ_{j<k} δ_{T^[j] y}` is a
`T`-invariant probability carried by `[a,b)`, different from `λ` because `λ` is atomless. That is the
form the Lean development uses (it avoids any measure-preservation statement for `K`).

**Corollary 4.10 ((H1) ⟹ (H2)).** If `λ` is the unique `T`-invariant probability measure carried by
`[a,b)` — hypothesis (H1) of §5 — then `L` has no periodic point in `(a,b]`.

*Proof.* Otherwise Lemma 4.9 produces a `T`-invariant probability `ν = λ|_K/λ(K)` with mass `1` on
`[a,b)` and `ν ≠ λ` (as `ν(K) = 1` and `λ(K) < 1`), contradicting (H1). ∎

Three comments.

* **This is the classical "periodic orbits come in families" phenomenon**, in its sharp form: not
  only a periodic *point* but the left-limit cycle `x₀, L x₀, …` generates a whole interval that is
  permuted by `T`, so a periodic left limit is a *periodic interval*, and a periodic interval is a
  non-trivial invariant Lebesgue measure. Nothing about connections, minimality or the source's
  §5.1–5.3 is used; the proof is 6 lines and purely one-dimensional.
* **Sharpness.** §8.3 shows that a periodic left limit does break uniform convergence; so Lemma
  4.9/Corollary 4.10 is exactly what makes `(H2)` disappear: the case where the conclusion of
  Theorem 2 would fail is the case where (H1) already fails.
* **Not needed, but true:** `(H2)` also holds for `simplexVolume d`-almost every length vector, by
  a completely different (linear-algebraic) argument; see the appendix, §6. The formalisation does
  not need it.

### 4.5 `T̃` restricted to `[a+, b−]` *is* uniquely ergodic — the source's claim, made precise

The space `X` of §2 doubles the two endpoints of the interval as well, and `T̃` fixes the two extra
points `leftGerm a` and `rightGerm b`, which are isolated (Lemma 2.4(vi), Corollary 2.6). That is an
artefact of the bookkeeping, and it is the only reason `T̃` fails to be uniquely ergodic on the whole
of `X`. On the correct space — the interval with only the **interior** split points doubled, i.e.
`X° = [a+, b−]` — the source's statement is true:

**Theorem 4.11 (unique ergodicity of the germ homeomorphism).** Assume (H1) (hence (H2), by
Corollary 4.10). Then `X°` is a nonempty compact space, `T̃` maps `X°` into `X°` continuously
(Corollary 2.6, Lemma 3.3), and the only `T̃`-invariant Borel probability measure on `X°` is the
lift `rightGerm_* λ`.

*Proof.* `X°` is closed in the compact space `X`, hence compact, and nonempty (`rightGerm a ∈ X°`).
Extend a probability `ν` on `X°` by `0` to `X`; since `T̃ (X°) ⊆ X°` and `ν` vanishes off `X°`, the
identity `ν A = ν ((T̃|_{X°})⁻¹ A)` for Borel `A ⊆ X°` gives `ν A = ν (T̃ ⁻¹' A)` for Borel
`A ⊆ X`, i.e. `ν` is `T̃`-invariant on `X` with `ν X° = 1`. So `proj_*ν = λ` by Theorem 4.6, whence
`ν = rightGerm_*λ` by Corollary 4.7. Conversely `rightGerm_*λ` is a `T̃`-invariant probability on
`X°` (Lemma 4.8, and `λ{b} = 0`). ∎

**Consequence for the proof of Theorem 2 (§5).** With Theorem 4.11 the source's argument becomes
literally valid: apply Tool 1 (Blueprint 1, Theorem 1.1) to the compact space `X°` and the
continuous map `T̃|_{X°}`, whose unique invariant probability measure is `rightGerm_*λ`; for
`ψ : ℝ → ℝ` continuous, `φ := ψ ∘ proj|_{X°}` is continuous, and
`∫ φ d(rightGerm_*λ) = ∫ψ dλ` because `proj ∘ rightGerm = id`. This is the same conclusion as
Theorem 1.2 gives, and §5 records both routes.

---

## 5. The theorem for interval exchanges

**Theorem 2 (uniform Birkhoff convergence for an interval exchange).** Let `T` be an interval
exchange on `[a,b)` in the sense of §1.1, let `λ := volume.restrict (Ico a b)`, and assume

  (H1) `λ` is the unique `T`-invariant probability measure `μ` on `ℝ` with `μ (Ico a b) = 1`
       (the conclusion of `masurVeech_ae_unique_invariant_perm`, after restriction).

Then for every `ψ : ℝ → ℝ` continuous and every `ε > 0` there is `N ≥ 1` such that for all
`n ≥ N` and all `x ∈ [a,b)`

  `|(1/n) Σ_{i<n} ψ (T^[i] x) − ∫ y, ψ y ∂λ| ≤ ε`.

**No hypothesis on the left limit is needed**: `L` automatically has no periodic point in `(a,b)`
by Corollary 4.10.

*Proof.* Two routes; both are the same compactness argument, and the first is literally the
source's.

**Route 1 (the source's, via Theorem 4.11).** By Corollary 4.10, (H1) gives `(H2)`. So, by Theorem
4.11, `X°` is a nonempty compact space, `T̃|_{X°} : X° → X°` is continuous, and its only invariant
probability measure is `μ° := rightGerm_* λ`. Apply Theorem 1.1 (Blueprint 1) to `X°`, `T̃|_{X°}`,
`μ°` and `φ := ψ ∘ proj|_{X°}` (continuous, `proj` being continuous): for every `ε > 0` there is
`N ≥ 1` with

  `|(1/n) Σ_{i<n} φ ((T̃|_{X°})^[i] z) − ∫ φ dμ°| ≤ ε`  for all `n ≥ N` and all `z ∈ X°`.

For `x ∈ [a,b)` take `z := rightGerm x ∈ X°`: by Lemma 3.2, `(T̃|_{X°})^[i] (rightGerm x) =
rightGerm (T^[i] x)`, so `φ ((T̃|_{X°})^[i] z) = ψ (T^[i] x)`; and `∫ φ dμ° = ∫ ψ d(proj_*μ°) =
∫ψ dλ` because `proj ∘ rightGerm = id` and `λ{b} = 0`. That is the statement.

**Route 2 (the relative form).** The same, packaged as Theorem 1.2 (Blueprint 1) with `X := X°`,
`f := T̃|_{X°}`, `Ω := rightGerm '' [a,b) ⊆ X°`, `φ := ψ ∘ proj`, `c := ∫ψ dλ`: conditions (a)
`f Ω ⊆ Ω` is Lemma 3.2, and (b) "every invariant probability with `ν (closure Ω) = 1` gives the
integral `c`" is Theorem 4.6 plus `Measure.integral_map`. Note `closure Ω = X°` (Lemma 2.4(vi)) and
`ψ` is bounded on `[a,b]`. ∎

**Remarks.**
* The proof never uses that the *cells* are clopen in `X`; it only uses that `ψ ∘ proj` is
  continuous, which is true for every continuous `ψ` because `proj` is continuous. The source's
  remark on the cells is correct if one reads the "cell" as the clopen *germ* set
  `{z : c < proj z < c'} ∪ {rightGerm c} ∪ {leftGerm c'}` (all cell endpoints lie in `D`), but the
  campaign does not need it: `UniqueErgodicFun` quantifies over continuous `ψ` only.
* (H1) is stated for measures with `μ (Ico a b) = 1`; the transfer produces a measure `ρ` on
  `[a,b]`, and §4.2 checks `ρ {b} = 0`, so (H1) applies.
* If the interval is `[0,1)` and `λ = unitMeas`, then `∫ y, ψ y ∂λ` is literally the integral that
  appears in `UniqueErgodicFun`.

---

## 6. Appendix (not needed): (H2) holds for almost every length vector, by a second argument

This section is **not on the critical path**: Corollary 4.10 derives `(H2)` from unique
ergodicity, so neither the hyperplane argument below nor Lemma 6.2 is needed for Theorem 2 or for
`MasurVeechFun`. It is kept because it is an independent proof of the same statement (with a
different hypothesis: it needs no unique ergodicity), because the combinatorial lemma 6.2 is a
pleasant sharp statement, and because the formalisation may skip it wholesale (§9, §11).

### 6.1 The statement

Fix `d ≥ 2` and `π : Equiv.Perm (Fin d)`. For `lam ∈ ℝ^d` with `∑ lam = 1` let `T_lam := mkIETFun lam π 0`
(so `a = 0`, `b = 1`) and `L_lam` its left-limit map (Definition 1.1, with the cut set
`mkIETCuts lam 0 1`).

**Proposition 6.1.** If `π` is irreducible, then `{lam : (H2) fails for T_lam}` is contained in a
countable union of proper hyperplanes of `{lam : ∑ lam = 1}`, hence has `simplexVolume d`-measure
zero.

### 6.2 The reduction to hyperplanes

For a finite word `w : Fin k → Fin d` write `m_α(w) := #{i < k : w i = α}`, and let

  `δ_α(lam) := imageLeft π lam α − leftEnd lam α = Σ_β lam_β (1_{π β < π α} − 1_{β < α})`

be the translation vector (`translationVector`). `T_lam` translates each cell by `δ_α`, and the
left-limit map `L` satisfies

  `L x = x + δ_α`  for `x ∈ (c_α, c_{α+1}]`,  and  `L a = a`,

where `c_0 = a < c_1 < … < c_d = b` are the cuts (`mkIETCuts lam 0 1`). Note the half-open
convention: for the *left* limit the point `c_α` belongs to the cell on its left, i.e. to
`(c_{α−1}, c_α]`, which is why the cells are written `(c_α, c_{α+1}]` here and `[c_α, c_{α+1})`
for `T` itself. Both statements follow from Lemma 1.2(ii) with the explicit formula
`L x = x + (T c − c)`, `c` the largest cut below `x`.

If `L^[k] x = x` for some `x ∈ (0,1]` and `k ≥ 1`, let `w i` be the cell `(c_{α}, c_{α+1}]`
containing `L^[i] x` (well defined because `x > 0` and the cells cover `(0,1]`). Then
`x = L^[k] x = x + Σ_{i<k} δ_{w i}`, i.e.

  `Σ_α m_α(w) δ_α(lam) = 0`.   (6.1)

Conversely, whether a solution `x` of (6.1) exists for the given word is a condition on `lam`
that we do not need to analyse: (6.1) alone already confines `lam` to the hyperplane
`H(w) := {lam : Σ_α m_α(w)δ_α(lam) = 0}`. Since there are countably many words,

  `{lam : (H2) fails} ⊆ ⋃_{k ≥ 1} ⋃_{w : Fin k → Fin d} H(w)`.

Each `H(w)` is defined by the linear equation `⟨c(w), lam⟩ = 0` with
`c(w)_β = Σ_α m_α(w) (1_{πβ < πα} − 1_{β < α}) ∈ ℤ`. It is a proper hyperplane (i.e. `c(w) ≠ 0`,
so `H(w) ≠ ℝ^d`) by:

**Lemma 6.2 (the combinatorial lemma).** Let `d ≥ 2`, `π` irreducible and `m : Fin d → ℕ` with
`m ≠ 0`. Then `c(m) ≠ 0`.

*Proof (complete).* Write `I_j := {0,…,j}` for `-1 ≤ j ≤ d−1` (so `I_{-1} = ∅`), and for
`m : Fin d → ℝ` put `m(J) := Σ_{α ∈ J}m_α`, `M := m(univ)`. First, an identity: for every `m` and
every `β`,

  `c(m)_β = Σ_{α : πα > πβ}m_α − Σ_{α > β}m_α = (M − m(π⁻¹(I_{πβ}))) − (M − m(I_β)) = m(I_β) − m(π⁻¹(I_{πβ}))`,

so `c(m) = 0` is equivalent to

  (T)  `m(I_β) = m(π⁻¹(I_{πβ}))`  for every `β`.

Suppose `c(m) = 0` with `m ≥ 0`, `m ≠ 0`, and let `S := supp m`, `f := min S`; note
`m(J) = 0 ⟺ J ∩ S = ∅`, which is all that non-negativity is used for.

*Step 1.* At `β = f`: `m(I_f) = m_f` (as `f = min S`) and `f ∈ π⁻¹(I_{πf})`; so the set
`π⁻¹(I_{πf})` has the same `m`-mass as the singleton `{f}` it contains, hence contains no other
point of `S`. Thus `π s > π f` for every `s ∈ S`, `s ≠ f`: `g := π f = min π(S)`.

*Step 2.* For every `β`: `πβ < g ⟺ β < f`. If `β < f` then `I_β ∩ S = ∅`, so `m(I_β) = 0`, so by
(T) `m(π⁻¹(I_{πβ})) = 0`, so no support point has `π`-image `≤ πβ`, in particular `πβ < πf = g`.
Conversely, if `πβ < g = min π(S)` then `π⁻¹(I_{πβ})` meets no support point, so (T) gives
`m(I_β) = 0`, i.e. `β < f`.

*Step 3.* Consequently `π⁻¹(I_{g−1}) = {β : πβ < g} = I_{f−1}`. Comparing cardinalities (`π` is
injective on the finite set) gives `g = f`, i.e. `π f = f`, and then `π(I_{f−1}) = I_{f−1}`.

Now `f ≥ 1` makes `I_{f−1}` a nonempty proper initial segment (`f ≤ d−1`, so `f−1 ≤ d−2`) mapped
into itself, contradicting irreducibility; and `f = 0` gives `π 0 = 0`, so `I_0` is a proper
initial segment mapped into itself (`0 ≤ d−2` as `d ≥ 2`), again a contradiction. Hence
`c(m) ≠ 0`. ∎

Three remarks, all verified.

* **Sharp form (any `π`).** For an arbitrary permutation, `{m ≥ 0, m ≠ 0 : c(m) = 0} ≠ ∅` iff
  `∃ f, π f = f ∧ π(I_{f−1}) = I_{f−1}`: the forward direction is Steps 1–3, and the converse takes
  `m = e_f`, for which `c(e_f)_β = 1[πβ < πf] − 1[β < f] = 1[β<f] − 1[β<f] = 0`. So irreducibility
  is *exactly* the right hypothesis and no counterexample can exist; the obstruction is "a fixed
  point sitting on top of an invariant initial segment".
* **No integrality is needed:** the argument gives `ker(Ω^t) ∩ ℝ_{≥0}^d = {0}` for irreducible `π`.
  Also `d ≥ 2` is used exactly at `f = 0` (for `d = 1`, `m = (1)` is a counterexample).
* **Where the content is.** If `m > 0` on every letter, (T) is immediate: with
  `σ(j) := m({j,…,d−1})` and `τ(j) := m(π⁻¹({j,…,d−1}))` (both strictly decreasing, `σ(0) = τ(0) = M`,
  `σ(d) = τ(d) = 0`), (T) says `τ(πβ+1) = σ(β+1)`, so `β ↦ πβ + 1 = (τ⁻¹∘σ)(β+1)` is increasing,
  i.e. `π = id`, which is reducible. So all the content is in the *zeros* of `m`, handled by Step 1.

*Machine checks (independent of the proof, not needed for it).* Exhaustive over all irreducible `π`
and all `m` with entries `≤ 4` (`d ≤ 4`), `≤ 3` (`d ≤ 5`), `≤ 2` (`d = 6`), all `0/1` supports for
`d ≤ 7`, and all cases with `c(m) = 0` including reducible `π` (the Lemma's full conclusion): zero
failures. Scripts `.ultramath/smvz4odkr/m3/verify*.py` and `.scratch/ref_swarm.py`.

*History.* This lemma was the one open point of the first version of this blueprint; it was proved
in the round of `.ultramath/smvz4odkr` (member `m3`), and the proof was checked by the referee
against the scripts above.

### 6.3 From hyperplanes to null sets


A proper hyperplane of `{lam : ∑ lam = 1}` has `simplexVolume d`-measure zero. Indeed
`simplexVolume d` is the pushforward of `volume.restrict (simplexRegion d)` under the affine map
`simplexMap d`, which is injective with image the simplex; the preimage of `{⟨c, lam⟩ = 0}` under
`simplexMap` is a proper affine hyperplane of `ℝ^{d-1}` (properness: `c ≠ 0` and `simplexMap` is
injective with affine image), and a proper affine hyperplane of `ℝ^n` is Lebesgue-null. Countable
unions of null sets are null. ∎

---

## 7. From `masurVeech_ae_unique_invariant_perm` to `MasurVeechFun`

**Theorem 3.** `MasurVeechFun` holds.

*Proof.* Let `d ≥ 2`, `[NeZero d]`, `π : Equiv.Perm (Fin d)` irreducible. We must show that for
`simplexVolume d`-almost every `lam : Fin d → ℝ≥0`, `UniqueErgodicFun (mkIETFun lam π 0)`.

By `masurVeech_ae_unique_invariant_perm hn π hπ` and `ae_mem_simplexOn_of_card_ne_zero`, for a.e.
`lam` the two conditions

  (0) `lam ∈ simplexOn (Fin d)`, i.e. `∑ lam = 1` (`ae_mem_simplexOn_of_card_ne_zero`);
  (i) `∀ h : lam ∈ simplexOn (Fin d), ∃! μ : ProbabilityMeasure ℝ,`
      `Invariant μ (mkIET1 lam π h) ∧ (μ : Measure ℝ) (Ico 0 1) = 1` (Masur–Veech)

hold simultaneously. **Nothing else is needed**: no condition on the left limit (that is Corollary
4.10, at *every* `lam`, which is why the appendix §6 is unused), and not even the positivity of the
coordinates — degenerate cells (`lam i = 0`) are allowed by `IsCutSet` (`isCutSet_mkIETCuts` does not
ask for positivity), and Lemma 1.8, Lemma 4.9 and Theorem 2 never use it. (Positivity would only
make the cells non-degenerate, which is a convenience, not a requirement.)

From (0), `mkIETFun lam π 0` is a bijection of `ℝ` fixing the complement of `[0,1)` and
mapping `[0,1)` onto itself, with cut set `mkIETCuts lam 0 1`: it is an interval exchange in the
sense of §1.1 (`isCutSet_mkIETCuts` for the cut set, `mkIETFun_inv_left` for the bijectivity).

Fix such a `lam` and let `h` be the proof of `lam ∈ simplexOn (Fin d)` (unique as a `Prop`). By (i)
and `IETDatum₂.ofPerm_toIET` the unique invariant probability measure of `T := mkIET1 lam π h` with
mass `1` on `[0,1)` is `Assembly.lebesgue` (Lebesgue on `[0,1)`), which is invariant by
`Assembly.invariant_unitMeas`. This is hypothesis (H1) of Theorem 2 with `[a,b) = [0,1)`.

Let `ψ : ℝ → ℝ` be continuous and `ε > 0`. Theorem 2 gives `N ≥ 1` with
`|(1/n)Σ_{i<n} ψ (T^[i] x) − ∫ψ dλ| ≤ ε` for `n ≥ N`, `x ∈ [0,1)`. Since `T` as a *function* is
`mkIETFun lam π 0` (`IETDatum₂.coe_mkIET1`, `toEquiv_mkIET1`: `⇑(mkIET1 lam π h) = mkIETFun lam π 0`,
definitionally) and `∫ y, ψ y ∂λ = ∫ y, ψ y ∂unitMeas` (`unitMeas = volume.restrict (Ico 0 1)`),
this is exactly `UniqueErgodicFun (mkIETFun lam π 0)`. ∎

**Bookkeeping.** `simplexVolume d` is a probability measure on `Fin d → ℝ≥0`; the a.e. statements
about `lam ∈ simplexOn` and about `lam` outside hyperplanes are combined with
`Filter.Eventually.and` and `Filter.eventually_of_forall`. The step "a.e. `lam` has all coordinates
`> 0`" is the a.e. statement that `simplexVolume d {lam : ∃ i, lam i = 0} = 0`: the set is the
image under `simplexMap` of a finite union of hyperplanes of `simplexRegion`, hence null.

---

## 8. Gap report on the source, and what replaces each sentence

### 8.1 "The i.e.m. T induces on Ĩ a homeomorphism T̃"

Correct, but only after fixing what "splitting" means: `T̃` cannot both be a homeomorphism and
satisfy `p ∘ T̃ = T ∘ p` everywhere, because at a cut `c` a net `y ↑ c` converges in `Ĩ` to the
left germ of `c`, and `T y → L c ≠ T c`. The correct statement (Lemma 3.2) is that `T̃` is the
**germ map**: right germs go to right germs of `T x`, left germs to left germs of `L x`, and
`p (T̃ z) = T (p z)` holds **on right germs only**. Everything downstream uses only right germs.
The split set also has to be the *full* orbit closure `⋃_{n ∈ ℤ} T^n (s ∪ s' ∪ {b})` (not the
one-sided unions written in the source, which happen to coincide with it — see below), otherwise
`T̃` is not continuous: continuity at a split point of the set requires that its image be split too.

*The source's set is the same as `D`.* `⋃_{n ≥ 0}T^n s' ∪ ⋃_{n ≥ 0}T^{-n} s = ⋃_{n ∈ ℤ}T^n(s ∪ s')`
because `T s ⊆ s'` and `T⁻¹ s' ⊆ s`: `T` maps a cut to the left end of the image of the cell on its
right, which is a singularity of `T⁻¹`. Adding `{b}` is necessary: `b` is a discontinuity point of
`T` (from the left, whenever the last cell is not translated by `0`) and of `T⁻¹`.

### 8.2 "which is easily seen to be uniquely ergodic when T is"

**True on the right space, and not "easily".** On the space `X° = [a+, b−]` of Theorem 4.11 — the
interval with only the interior singularities doubled — `T̃` is indeed uniquely ergodic when `T` is,
and the unique invariant measure is the lift of `λ`. Three things have to be said about the sentence
as printed.

1. **The space matters.** If one doubles the two endpoints of the interval as well (which is what
   §2 does for bookkeeping convenience, since `a ∈ s` and `b` is needed in the split set), then `T̃`
   fixes the two extra isolated points `leftGerm a` and `rightGerm b` (Lemma 2.4(vi), Corollary 2.6),
   so on that space `T̃` is *not* uniquely ergodic. Those two points are artefacts: they are the
   one-sided germs of the endpoints, never approached from inside `[a,b)`. This is why the split set
   must contain the interior singularities and their orbits, and why the space to which "uniquely
   ergodic" applies is the interval with only the interior points doubled (Remark 2.7, Theorem 4.11).
2. **The proof is not "easy".** Unique ergodicity of `T̃|_{X°}` is Theorem 4.11, and it rests on the
   defect identity (Lemma 4.4), the "mass is constant along an orbit" lemma (Lemma 4.3), the lift
   lemma (Lemma 4.1) and property (H2) — which is *automatic*, by the periodic-interval argument of
   §4.4, but is not vacuous. In particular the L-germs at the jumps could a priori carry an invariant
   measure (that is what would break the transfer), and it is Corollary 4.10 that rules it out.
3. **The mechanism.** The one place where the invariant measure *could* differ from the lift of `λ`
   is a `T̃`-invariant measure charging the left germ of a jump point; the defect identity computes
   exactly that defect. So the honest one-line summary is: "`T̃` is uniquely ergodic because `T` is,
   the only possible defect being an invariant measure on a periodic left limit, which unique
   ergodicity forbids".

### 8.3 A periodic left limit *would* break the theorem (this is why §4.4 matters)

Suppose `L` has a periodic point `x₀ ∈ (a,b)`, of period `k ≥ 1`, and let `x₀, …, x_{k-1}` be its
`L`-orbit. Then the conclusion of Theorem 2 **fails** for this `T` — so `(H2)` is not a technical
convenience, and Lemma 4.9 is the exact reason it never has to be assumed. Here is the argument.

For `n ≥ 1` let `A_n := (1/n) Σ_{i<n} ψ (proj (T̃^[i] ·)) : X → ℝ`. Each `A_n` is continuous on
`X` (Lemmas 2.4 and 3.3 and continuity of `ψ`). On right germs, `A_n (rightGerm y) = (1/n) Σ_{i<n} ψ (T^[i] y)`
(Lemma 3.2). On the *left* germ of `x₀`, Lemma 3.5 gives
`proj (T̃^[i] (leftGerm x₀)) = L^[i] x₀ = x_{i mod k}`, hence

  `A_n (leftGerm x₀) = (1/n) Σ_{i<n} ψ x_{(i mod k)}  →  (1/k) Σ_{j<k} ψ x_j =: c'  (n → ∞)`.

Now `leftGerm x₀ = lim_{y ↑ x₀} rightGerm y` (Lemma 2.4(v)), and `x₀ ∈ (a,b)` means that there are
`y ∈ [a,b)` arbitrarily close below `x₀`, so `leftGerm x₀` is a limit point of right germs.
If the averages converged to `c := ∫ψ dλ` uniformly on `Ω = rightGerm '' [a,b)`, then for every
`ε > 0` and all `n ≥ N(ε)` one would have `|A_n (rightGerm y) − c| ≤ ε` for all `y`, hence, letting
`y ↑ x₀` and using the continuity of `A_n`, also `|A_n (leftGerm x₀) − c| ≤ ε`; letting `n → ∞`
gives `|c' − c| ≤ ε` for every `ε`, i.e. `c' = c`. So `(1/k) Σ_j ψ x_j = ∫ ψ dλ` for every
continuous `ψ`, i.e. `(1/k) Σ_j δ_{x_j} = λ` — impossible, since `λ` has no atoms.

Two conclusions. First, `(H2)` is genuinely necessary for the conclusion, so a proof of the theorem
must either assume it or derive it — it cannot simply be ignored. Second, the failure is invisible
at the level of `λ`-a.e. `x` (it is a failure of *uniformity*, produced by the orbits starting just
below `x₀`), which is why an a.e. version of `(H2)` would also have sufficed; Corollary 4.10 gives
the pointwise version instead, and costs six lines.

### 8.4 "the interval I^t_α corresponds to a clopen set in Ĩ"

True with the right reading: the *germ closure* `{z : c_α < proj z < c_{α+1}} ∪ {rightGerm c_α} ∪
{leftGerm c_{α+1}}` is clopen (its complement is described by the opposite inequalities), whereas
`{z : proj z ∈ [c_α, c_{α+1})}` is not (at `leftGerm c_{α+1}` the value jumps). Nothing depends on
this, since only continuous `ψ` are needed.

### 8.5 What the source does not say and a formalisation must

* `λ` is invariant (`Assembly.invariant_unitMeas`) and is the *unique* invariant measure carried by
  `[0,1)` — that is the input from Masur–Veech, not part of the trick.
* the lifting lemma (§4.1), whose content is that an atomless measure has at most one lift to the
  split space with a prescribed pushforward. This is where the "left/right" splitting pays: without
  it, a `T̃`-invariant measure could be a different lift of `λ` (a "one-sided" measure).
* the passage `ρ {b} = 0`, needed because (H1) is stated for measures with mass `1` on `[0,1)`.

### 8.6 Keane's theorem is not an equivalence, and the "no connection" route is not available

It is tempting to obtain `(H2)` as follows: *an IET that is uniquely ergodic is minimal; an IET that
is minimal has no connection (Keane); an IET with no connection has no periodic left limit; hence
`(H2)`*. The three implications need separate scrutiny, and the second one is false; it is worth
recording why, because the source's §5 invites exactly this reading.

1. **"No connection ⟹ minimal" is Theorem 5.9 of the source** (Keane), article p. 17: *"If an
   i.e.m. has no connection, it is minimal."* It is **not** an equivalence. Yoccoz's own
   Exercise 5.11, immediately below it on the same page, says: *"For d = 2, T is minimal iff there
   is no connection … For d ≥ 3, show that there exists T minimal but having a connection, and also
   T with no connection but lengths data rationally dependent."* So for `d ≥ 3` **minimality does
   not imply the absence of connections**, and any argument that uses Keane's theorem in that
   direction is invalid. (For `d = 2` the equivalence does hold, which is presumably where the
   impression comes from; and `d ≥ 2` is the range of `MasurVeechFun`, so the `d ≥ 3` case is the
   relevant one.)
2. **"Uniquely ergodic ⟹ minimal"** is, I believe, true, but the proof is not immediate: the natural
   argument (take a minimal component `K`, show `λ|_K` is invariant, contradicting uniqueness)
   requires the structure theory of IETs — that the minimal components are finite unions of
   intervals — and the degenerate case `K ∩ J ≠ ∅` has to be handled. Nothing in the present
   blueprint needs it, and I do not have a self-contained proof to put here.
3. **"No connection ⟹ no periodic left limit"** is true and provable (a periodic left-limit cycle
   either contains a jump point, and then a connection, or it is a `T`-periodic orbit, and then the
   classical "periodic intervals come in families" gives a connection). But it is *weaker* than
   what is needed, and — more importantly — the hypothesis "no connection" is not available for a
   general uniquely ergodic `T` by steps 1–2.

What actually works is **not** any of this: a periodic left limit directly produces a *periodic
interval* and hence a non-trivial invariant Lebesgue measure, contradicting unique ergodicity on
the nose. That is Lemma 4.9/Corollary 4.10, six lines, and it uses neither minimality, nor
Keane's theorem, nor connections. Keane's theorem is therefore **not on the critical path** of this
blueprint and is not formalised here; if it is wanted elsewhere in the project (it is, for
instance, the source's route to minimality in the Keane condition), the true statement is
Theorem 5.9 with the proof of the source's §5.1–5.3, and the failure of the converse should be
recorded with it.

### 9.3 `Limits.lean` — §1

```lean
variable {a b : ℝ} {s : Finset ℝ}

-- the exchange is a bijection, so state everything for an `Equiv` (this is what `IET a b` is)
variable {e : ℝ ≃ ℝ}

theorem tendsto_nhdsGT (h : IsCutSet (⇑e) a b s) {x : ℝ} (hx : x ∈ Set.Ico a b) :
    Tendsto (⇑e) (𝓝[>] x) (𝓝 (e x))

/-- the largest cut strictly below `x` -/
noncomputable def cellLeftBelow (h : IsCutSet (⇑e) a b s) (x : ℝ) (hx : a < x) : ℝ

noncomputable def leftLimitFun (h : IsCutSet (⇑e) a b s) (x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  if hx : a < x then x + (e (cellLeftBelow h x hx) - cellLeftBelow h x hx) else x

theorem tendsto_nhdsLT_leftLimit (h : IsCutSet (⇑e) a b s) {x : ℝ} (hx : x ∈ Set.Ioc a b) :
    Tendsto (⇑e) (𝓝[<] x) (𝓝 (leftLimitFun h x))

theorem leftLimitFun_mem (h : IsCutSet (⇑e) a b s) {x : ℝ} (hx : x ∈ Set.Icc a b) :
    leftLimitFun h x ∈ Set.Icc a b

theorem leftLimitFun_eq_apply_of_notMem (h : IsCutSet (⇑e) a b s) {x : ℝ} (hx : x ∉ s) :
    leftLimitFun h x = e x                       -- `L = T` off the cuts

theorem isCutSet_symm (h : IsCutSet (⇑e) a b s) :
    ∃ s' : Finset ℝ, IsCutSet (⇑(e.symm)) a b s'  -- or: `mkIETCuts (imageLengths …)`, see below
```

Two ways to get `IsCutSet` for the inverse: (i) abstractly from `IsCutSet` + the image-cell API
(`IsCutSet.image_cell`, `Equiv.IsIET.image_cells_union`), (ii) concretely for
`T = mkIETFun lam π a`, where `mkIETEquiv lam π a` is an `Equiv` whose inverse is
`mkIETEquiv (imageLengths π lam) π.symm a` (`mkIETFun_inv_left`) and `isCutSet_mkIETCuts` applies to
`imageLengths π lam`. (ii) is cheaper and is enough for the campaign; state the abstract version
only if it costs nothing.

```lean
/-- the split set; `e` is the exchange as an equiv, so that `e ^ n` makes sense for `n : ℤ` -/
noncomputable def splitSet (e : ℝ ≃ ℝ) (s s' : Finset ℝ) (a b : ℝ) : Set ℝ :=
  ⋃ n : ℤ, (⇑(e ^ n)) '' ((s : Set ℝ) ∪ (s' : Set ℝ) ∪ {b})

theorem splitSet_countable … : (splitSet e s s' a b).Countable
theorem image_splitSet … : ⇑e '' splitSet e s s' a b = splitSet e s s' a b
theorem leftLimitFun_image_splitSet … : leftLimitFun h '' splitSet … ⊆ splitSet …

/-- **(H2)**, as a predicate (proved from unique ergodicity in `Transfer.lean`, §4.4) -/
def NoPeriodicLeftLimit (h : IsCutSet (⇑e) a b s) : Prop :=
  ∀ (k : ℕ), 0 < k → ∀ x ∈ Set.Ioc a b, (leftLimitFun h)^[k] x ≠ x

/-- **Lemma 4.9**: a periodic left limit generates a periodic interval. -/
theorem exists_periodic_interval (h : IsCutSet (⇑e) a b s) {x₀ : ℝ} (hx₀ : x₀ ∈ Set.Ioc a b)
    {k : ℕ} (hk : 0 < k) (hper : (leftLimitFun h)^[k] x₀ = x₀) :
    ∃ ε > 0, ∃ K : Set ℝ, MeasurableSet K ∧ K ⊆ Set.Ico a b ∧ 0 < volume K ∧ volume K < 1 ∧
      (⇑e) '' K = K ∧ ∀ A, MeasurableSet A → volume (((⇑e)⁻¹' A) ∩ K) = volume (A ∩ K)

/-- **Corollary 4.10**: unique ergodicity forbids periodic left limits. -/
theorem noPeriodicLeftLimit_of_unique (h : IsCutSet (⇑e) a b s)
    (hH1 : ∀ μ : ProbabilityMeasure ℝ, (μ : Measure ℝ).map (⇑e) = (μ : Measure ℝ) →
      (μ : Measure ℝ) (Set.Ico a b) = 1 → (μ : Measure ℝ) = volume.restrict (Set.Ico a b)) :
    NoPeriodicLeftLimit h
```

### 9.4 `Split.lean` — §2

```lean
def SplitI (a b : ℝ) (D : Set ℝ) : Type

namespace SplitI
instance : TopologicalSpace (SplitI a b D)      -- induced from ℝ × (D → Bool)
instance [Countable D] : CompactSpace (SplitI a b D)
instance : T2Space (SplitI a b D)
instance [Countable D] : PseudoMetrizableSpace (SplitI a b D)
instance [Countable D] : BorelSpace (SplitI a b D)

def proj : SplitI a b D → ℝ
theorem continuous_proj : Continuous proj
theorem proj_mem : ∀ z, proj z ∈ Set.Icc a b
def rightGerm (x : ℝ) (hx : x ∈ Set.Icc a b) : SplitI a b D
def leftGerm  (x : ℝ) (hx : x ∈ Set.Icc a b) : SplitI a b D
theorem proj_rightGerm / proj_leftGerm
theorem rightGerm_eq_leftGerm (hx : x ∉ D) : rightGerm x … = leftGerm x …
theorem eq_rightGerm_or_leftGerm : ∀ z, z = rightGerm (proj z) … ∨ z = leftGerm (proj z) …
theorem tendsto_rightGerm_nhdsLT (x ∈ Icc a b) : Tendsto (rightGerm ·) (𝓝[<] x) (𝓝 (leftGerm x))
theorem rightGerm_dense : closure (range (rightGerm ·)) = univ \ {leftGerm a, rightGerm b}
/-- the one-sided open sets of 2.3 -/
def upSet (x : ℝ) : Set (SplitI a b D)
def downSet (x : ℝ) : Set (SplitI a b D)
theorem isOpen_upSet / isOpen_downSet
theorem upSet_subset : z ∈ upSet x → x ≤ proj z
```

### 9.5 `Germ.lean` — §3

```lean
def germMap (h : IsCutSet T a b s) (L : ℝ → ℝ) : SplitI a b D → SplitI a b D
theorem germMap_mem …
theorem continuous_germMap … : Continuous (germMap h L)
theorem germMap_rightGerm : germMap h L (rightGerm x …) = rightGerm (T x) …
theorem germMap_injective …
theorem side_germMap / proj_germMap_leftGerm : proj (germMap h L (leftGerm x …)) = L x
```

### 9.6 `Transfer.lean` — §4

```lean
theorem existsUnique_lift (s : ℝ → SplitI a b D) (hs : ∀ x, proj (s x) = x)
    (hsB : Measurable s) (hD : D.Countable) (hλD : λ (D : Set ℝ) = 0)
    (hλatom : ∀ x, λ {x} = 0) {ν : Measure (SplitI a b D)} [IsProbabilityMeasure ν]
    (hpush : ν.map proj = λ) : ν = λ.map s

theorem mass_germMap_singleton (hν : ν.map (germMap h L) = ν) (z : SplitI a b D) :
    ν {germMap h L z} = ν {z}

theorem defect_identity (hν : ν.map (germMap h L) = ν) (g : ℝ →ᵇ ℝ) :
    ∫ x, g x ∂(ν.map proj) - ∫ x, g x ∂((ν.map proj).map (⇑e))
      = ∑ c ∈ (J : Finset ℝ), (ν {leftGerm c …}).toReal * (g (L c) - g (e c))

theorem lift_invariant : (λ.map (rightGerm ·)).map (germMap h L) = λ.map (rightGerm ·)

/-- the correct space `X° = [a+, b−]`: right germs of the half-open interval -/
def rightPart : Set (SplitI a b D) := closure (range (fun x : Set.Ico a b => rightGerm x …))

theorem transfer (hH2 : NoPeriodicLeftLimit h) (hν : ν.map (germMap h L) = ν)
    (hK : ν rightPart = 1) : ν.map proj = λ

/-- **Theorem 4.11**: `T̃` restricted to `[a+, b−]` is uniquely ergodic. -/
theorem uniqueErgodicOn_rightPart (hH2 : NoPeriodicLeftLimit h) :
    ∀ ν : ProbabilityMeasure (rightPart …), (ν : Measure _).map (germMap h L) = ν →
      ν = (λ.map (rightGerm ·)).comap …    -- stated on the subtype `rightPart` in practice
```

### 9.7 `IET.lean` — Theorem 2

```lean
theorem uniqueErgodicFun_of_isCutSet
    (h : IsCutSet (⇑e) a b s) (ha : a = 0) (hb : b = 1)
    (hH1 : ∀ μ : ProbabilityMeasure ℝ, (μ : Measure ℝ).map (⇑e) = (μ : Measure ℝ) →
             (μ : Measure ℝ) (Set.Ico a b) = 1 → (μ : Measure ℝ) = λ) :
    ∀ ψ : ℝ → ℝ, Continuous ψ → ∀ ε > 0, ∃ N : ℕ, 0 < N ∧ ∀ n ≥ N, ∀ x ∈ Set.Ico a b,
      |(n : ℝ)⁻¹ * ∑ i ∈ Finset.range n, ψ ((⇑e)^[i] x) - ∫ y, ψ y ∂λ| ≤ ε
```

This is the shape of `UniqueErgodicFun` with `[a,b) = [0,1)`. The blueprint proves the general
`a, b` version (§5); the campaign only needs `a = 0`, `b = 1`, and the general version costs nothing
(the proof never uses the specific endpoints). Note that `(H2)`, i.e. `NoPeriodicLeftLimit h`, is
**not** a hypothesis: it is obtained inside the proof from `hH1` via
`noPeriodicLeftLimit_of_unique` (§4.4). The proof is Theorem 1.1 (Blueprint 1) applied to
`T̃|_{X°}` on the compact space `rightPart` (Theorem 4.11) with `φ := ψ ∘ proj`; the relative form
of Blueprint 1 gives the same conclusion and is the cheaper packaging if `rightPart` as a subtype is
awkward.

### 9.8 `AeNoPeriodic.lean` — the appendix §6 (optional, **not needed**)

Lemma 6.2 and Proposition 6.1 are correct and proved in §6.2–6.3, but they are not used by any other

own sake (it is a pleasant sharp fact: for an arbitrary permutation a non-negative kernel vector
exists iff there is a fixed point `f` with `π(I_{f−1}) = I_{f−1}`).

```lean
/-- Lemma 6.2 (appendix; not on the critical path) -/
theorem linear_coeff_ne_zero (hπ : IsIrreduciblePerm π) {m : Fin d → ℕ} (hm : m ≠ 0) :
    (fun β => ∑ α, (m α : ℤ) * ((if π β < π α then 1 else 0) - (if β < α then 1 else 0))) ≠ 0
```

The a.e. statement is proved by exhibiting the bad set as a countable union of hyperplanes
(`Set.Countable.iUnion` of `MeasureTheory.Measure.volume (hyperplane) = 0`), each hyperplane of the
form `{lam | ⟨c, lam⟩ = 0}` with `c ≠ 0` from Lemma 6.2. Representing the simplex as the image of
`simplexRegion d` under the affine `simplexMap d` turns the statement into: a countable union of
proper hyperplanes of `ℝ^{d-1}` intersected with an open set is Lebesgue-null.

## 10. Traps and risks

1. **`T` versus `⇑T`.** `mkIET1 lam π h : IET 0 1` coerces to a function definitionally equal to
   `mkIETFun lam π 0` (`IETDatum₂.coe_mkIET1`, `toEquiv_mkIET1` are `rfl`). Use `coe_mkIET1` to
   rewrite rather than unfolding `mkIETFun`.
2. **`D` must contain `b` and must be `T`-invariant.** A one-sided split set makes `T̃`
   discontinuous at the images of split points; and `b` is a discontinuity of `T` from the left
   unless the last cell is translated by `0`.
3. **`L` must be defined at `a` and at `b`.** `L a = a` (from the identity off `[a,b)`), and
   `L b` is the right end of the image of the last cell. Forgetting `L a = a` breaks Lemma 3.3(a)
   at `leftGerm a`, which is however isolated, so the campaign's statements survive; but §4.2
   needs `L b`.
4. **Injectivity of `T̃` is needed, surjectivity is not.** Lemma 4.3 uses
   `ν {T̃ z} = ν {z}`, i.e. `T̃ ⁻¹' {T̃ z} = {z}`. Surjectivity is used only in the decorative
   Lemma 3.4; if the inverse map is expensive, prove injectivity alone.
5. **The `b`-fibre.** `ρ {b} = ν {leftGerm b} + ν {rightGerm b}`; both terms vanish, but for two
   different reasons (isolated point; (H2), which is now Corollary 4.10 applied at `x = b`). Keep
   them separate.
6. **`∫ ψ dλ` versus `∫ ψ dunitMeas`.** `λ` lives on `Ico a b`; `μ (Ico 0 1) = 1` in the
   Masur–Veech statement is what identifies the abstract invariant measure with `λ`.
7. **Zero lengths are harmless.** `simplexRegion` is open, so a.e. `lam` has all coordinates
   positive, but *nothing in the blueprint needs it*: `IsCutSet` allows degenerate cells, and
   Lemmas 1.8, 4.9 and Theorem 2 go through verbatim. Do not spend a lemma on it (and do not
   *assume* positivity silently either — `simplexVolume d` is concentrated on the simplex
   `{∑ lam = 1}`, and that is all that is used).
8. **`PseudoMetrizableSpace`/`BorelSpace` for `D → Bool`.** `Pi.borelSpace` needs `[Countable D]`
   and second-countable factors; `D.Countable` gives `[Countable D]` (`Set.Countable` →
   `Subtype.countable`), `Bool` is finite. Check both instances early: everything in §4 needs
   `BorelSpace (SplitI a b D)`.
9. **The one-sided neighbourhoods `U⁺ x`, `U⁻ x` of §2.3 must be stated with `proj` and `rightGerm`,
   not with `χ`, at points `x ∉ D`** (where the two germs coincide).
10. **Do not attempt the order topology.** The product description (§2.1) gives compactness,
    Hausdorff, pseudo-metrizability and Borel for free, and Lemmas 2.5/3.3 are stated in its
    coordinates.
11. **Negative iterates.** `D` is a union over `n : ℤ`, so `T` must be an `Equiv ℝ ℝ` (as `IET a b`
    is, extending `Equiv`) and `T^[n]` is `T.toEquiv ^ n` (`zpow`), not `Function.iterate`. The
    same for `T̃` in Lemma 3.4 (its inverse is only used there).
12. **`side` at unsplit points.** For `x ∉ D` there is a single point over `x` and `side` is a
    convention; every statement about `side` must be read modulo "or `proj z ∉ D`". In particular
    `side (leftGerm x) = false` and `side (rightGerm x) = true` only differ when `x ∈ D`.
13. **Lemma 4.9 needs the *closed* cells `(c_α, c_{α+1}]`, not `[c_α, c_{α+1})`.** The interval
    `J_i = (x_i − ε, x_i)` must satisfy `T y − y = L x_i − x_i` for all `y ∈ J_i`; this is
    `IsCutSet.transl_of_not_separated` applied to `(y, x_i)` once `ε ≤ x_i − c(x_i)`. With the
    other convention the translation on `[c_α, c_{α+1})` would give `L x_i = x_i`, which is false.
14. **Do not double the endpoints.** `X` doubles `a` and `b` as well (because `a ∈ s` and `b` is in
    the split set), which is harmless for compactness but produces the two isolated fixed points
    `leftGerm a` and `rightGerm b` of `T̃`. Every *dynamical* statement must be made on
    `X° = closure (rightGerm '' [a,b)) = X ∖ {leftGerm a, rightGerm b}`, which is compact, closed
    in `X`, `T̃`-invariant, and on which `T̃` is uniquely ergodic (Theorem 4.11). In particular the
    hypothesis of `transfer` is `ν X° = 1`, not `ν (closure (rightGerm '' [a,b])) = 1` — the latter
    is *false* for `ν = δ_{rightGerm b}`.

## 12. Dependency audit: what these two blueprints use from outside themselves

This section answers, in one place, the question "is anything admitted?".

### 12.1 The one mathematical input

`masurVeech_ae_unique_invariant_perm` (`MainTheorem.lean`), i.e. hypothesis
`(H1)`: for a.e. length vector the exchange has exactly one invariant probability measure carried by
`[0,1)`. It is *proved in this repository*, with the single axiom check
`[propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]`, and it is the theorem this round upgrades. No other
mathematical statement is assumed anywhere in Blueprint 1 or Blueprint 2.

### 12.2 Mathlib facts used

Blueprint 1 and 2 use, and nothing more than,

* `P(X)` is compact for `X` compact Hausdorff: `MeasureTheory.instCompactSpaceProbabilityMeasure`;
* weak convergence = convergence of integrals of bounded continuous functions:
  `ProbabilityMeasure.tendsto_iff_forall_integral_tendsto`;
* `∫ g d(ν.map f) = ∫ (g ∘ f) dν`: `MeasureTheory.Measure.integral_map`;
* two finite measures agreeing on a π-system generating the Borel σ-algebra agree:
  `MeasureTheory.Measure.ext_of_isPiSystem` (Lemma 4.1);
* two finite Borel measures on a pseudo-metrizable space agreeing on bounded continuous test
  functions agree: `MeasureTheory.ext_of_forall_integral_eq_of_IsFiniteMeasure`, available because
  `HasOuterApproxClosed` holds for every `PseudoMetrizableSpace` (Lemma 4.4, Theorem 4.6);
* the instance chain for the split space: `Pi.compactSpace`, `PseudoMetrizableSpace.subtype`,
  `PseudoMetrizableSpace.pi`, `Subtype.borelSpace`, `Prod.borelSpace`, `Pi.borelSpace`
  (the last needs `[Countable D]` and second-countable factors, both available);
* `birkhoffSum` / `birkhoffAverage` (`Dynamics/BirkhoffSum`), and
  `IsCutSet`-API from `CutSet.lean`, `CutSetMeasure.lean`, `IET.lean`
  (`cells_union`, `transl_of_not_separated`, `image_cells_union`, `mkIETFun_inv_left`,
  `isCutSet_mkIETCuts`, `Equiv.IsIET.measure_preimage`, `Assembly.invariant_unitMeas`);
* for the *appendix only*: a proper affine hyperplane of `ℝ^n` is Lebesgue-null, and Riesz
  representation (for the optional converse of Blueprint 1 §6).

### 12.3 What is *not* used

* **Keane's theorem.** Neither form: not "no connection ⇒ minimal" (which is the true one, Yoccoz
  Theorem 5.9), and certainly not "minimal ⇒ no connection" (false for `d ≥ 3`, Exercise 5.11). No
  step of any proof mentions minimality, connections, or the structure theory of IETs. See §8.6.
* **The appendix §6** (the a.e. hyperplane argument and Lemma 6.2). `(H2)` comes from §4.4 instead.
* **The converse in Blueprint 1 §6** (uniform convergence ⇒ unique ergodicity). Not needed.
* **Positivity of the lengths.** Not needed (§7 and trap 7).

### 12.4 What is stated but not proved in full

* Lemma 3.4's *surjectivity* clause. Injectivity is what is used (Lemma 4.3, Corollary 2.6); the
  surjectivity paragraph indicates the inverse (the germ map of `T⁻¹`) and the two identities needed,
  and can be dropped if one prefers to state only injectivity.
* Everything else in §§1–5 and §7 is proved, including the analytic input about the left limit
  (Lemma 1.8), which is where the first version of this blueprint had three unstated sub-lemmas.

So: the blueprint is self-contained modulo Masur–Veech (the repository's own theorem) and the
Mathlib facts above. It admits no ergodic-theoretic or IET-theoretic theorem, in particular not
Keane's, and the only hypothesis of the upgraded theorem is `(H1)`.

# Part III — what is gone

The pre-merge project held more than the nine documents of Part II, and it was deleted at the owner's
instruction on 2 November.  What it held besides the prose is not reproduced anywhere:

| what | what became of it |
|---|---|
| the pre-merge Lean sources and their own Lake project — `lakefile.toml`, `lake-manifest.json`, `lean-toolchain`, the umbrella module | their content is `IETFree/`, under the module names `IETFree.…`; the only duplicates were the three verbatim copies of the single-exchange API (Part I, Addendum 150) |
| the sealed-anchor records — `Rigidity/frozen-anchors.json` and `Rigidity/abi/{unit_meas_v1,is_rigid_v1,veech_rigidity_fun_v1,veeche_rigidity_v1}.txt` | **nothing is frozen any more**, and the manifest, the ABI texts and their hashes documented the earlier process only: they referred to paths in the pre-merge project, never to `IETFree/` |
| the guard scripts — `Rigidity/tools/{check-rigidity.py,lean-gate.sh}`, `sanity_check.py`, `vocabulary.sha256` | they ran against the pre-merge project, not against this tree |
| the counterexample `MainCounterexample.lean` | it showed that the unrestricted main statement is false: an exchange is the identity off `[0,1)`, so the Dirac mass at `2` is invariant besides Lebesgue's, at *every* point of the simplex.  The hypothesis `μ (Ico 0 1) = 1` in `MainTheorem.lean` is its repair, and the three docstrings that cited the file now state the argument |
| the survey PDF, the arXiv source of the distortion appendix and the marked-up transcription of it | working copies of the two sources; every passage that mattered is quoted in Part I (Addenda 89–105) and cited by page in the blueprints of Part II |

Its Lean modules are in `IETFree/`; its prose is Part II above.  `IET2/NOTES.md` is the present state;
this file is the archive.
